title: School and workplace policies, disclosure and records

sources.claim: US Department of Education Dear Colleague Letter (July 22, 2025): federal grant funds may support some AI uses (for example instructional materials and tutoring) when they meet program requirements, with attention to privacy, appropriate use and stakeholder involvement; it is guidance about funding, not a classroom rule. Schools set their own AI policies.

sections.skill: Follow a written AI policy, disclose AI help and keep records

questions.prompt: In this fictional policy, which use is allowed?

choices.text: Submitting a paragraph written by an AI tool as if the student had written it personally

questions.intro: Schools and workplaces often have WRITTEN AI POLICIES. Read yours: which tools are APPROVED, which uses are allowed (brainstorming, editing, coding help), which are not (submitting AI work as your own, entering private data), and whether you must DISCLOSE AI help and how. Keep RECORDS when required, such as saved drafts or a note of how AI was used. Policies differ between classes, schools and employers. In the US, the Department of Education issued guidance in July 2025 about using federal grant funds for some AI uses; it is guidance about funding, and schools still set their own AI policies.

sections.skill: Compare AI policies with rules for calculators in math class

questions.prompt: Are calculators allowed on every test?

choices.text: No; it depends on the test
Yes, calculators are allowed on every test in every class in every school, always

questions.correct_answer: No; it depends on the test
questions.intro: Some math tests allow CALCULATORS; others do not, and some allow only basic ones. A student who uses a graphing calculator on a "no calculator" test breaks the rule, even if calculators are allowed elsewhere. Teachers may also ask students to "show your work." AI policies work the same way: what is allowed depends on the class or job, and showing your work is like disclosing AI help and keeping records.

questions.prompt: A policy is unclear. What is the best way to record the answer you get?
questions.intro: When a policy is unclear or silent, ask before you act, and keep the answer in writing if possible. A policy for one class may not apply in another, and policies change over time. Disclosure is easier when you keep records as you go: drafts, prompts used, and what you changed. If you realize you broke a policy, telling the teacher or manager promptly is usually better than hoping it goes unnoticed.
